rows.english: Since the three types of suffering are mentioned later on in our root text, we'll describe them briefly. All impure feelings of pain constitute the first type of suffering: the "suffering of suffering."

rows.english: All impure feelings of pleasure constitute the second type of suffering: the "suffering of change." We can explain this suffering as follows. When you're in a place that's very hot, then something cool seems like pleasure. When you're in a place that's very cold, then something warm seems like pleasure. The same is true when you've had to walk a long way (sitting would seem a pleasure), or had to sit for a long time (walking would seem a pleasure).

Notes to Reading Ten 60 Go forth now and defeat them: These lines are found in the Great Fifth's famous presentation on the Steps of the path, entitled "Word of the Gentle One." They occur as a poetic interlude between sections of the work's prose philosophical presentation, a device favored as well by His Holiness the First Dalai Lama. "Mental afflictions" are essentially bad thoughts, and constitute a basic source of all our suffering. Their primary characteristic is to disturb our peace of mind, and linguistically as well their name in Sanskrit, klesha, comes from a verbal root meaning "to distress." Although the mental afflictions are nearly countless, the six primary ones are desire, anger, pride, ignorance, harmful doubt, and wrong views. See Prof. Whitney's Roots of the Sanskrit Language, and Kedrup Tenpa Dargye's "Overview of the Perfection of Wisdom." 61 Six forms of life: That is, the six different possible types of rebirth: as a hellbeing, a craving spirit, an animal, a human, someone nearly a pleasure being, or a full pleasure being. See also note 37. 62 Three different kinds of suffering: The illustrious Kedrup Tenpa Dargye explains them as follows in his Overview of the Perfection of Wisdom: What we call "pervasive" suffering is the subtle condition of change, the fact that the physical, mental, and other parts of ourselves which we have taken on cannot remain, but begin to change from the moment after they come into existence. rows.english: One may then pose another question: "Suppose the embryo in one woman's body is removed and placed in the womb of another, and the child takes birth from this woman's womb. Killing which of these two women would constitute the `immediate' misdeed?" The mother of the person in question is the former of the two women: the one whose menses he came from. Therefore killing this first woman would be the immediate misdeed; she played the principal role in providing the person a body fit for gaining freedom. We could not consider the second woman, the woman who kept the child in her womb, the child's mother--this act alone would not make hers the principal role.

The older commentary to the Twenty Verses on Vows, for example, states that The reason is that the vows of the bodhisattva can be included exhaustively into one or another of two groups of wrong deeds. First there are those included into the group of bad deeds which are similar to the major failures of the vows of ordination; and secondly there are those included into the group of bad deeds which are similar to the wrong activities which also constitute a category of the vows of ordination. rows.english: The Master though rebuts this position: This could never be correct--first because of the incongruity between the being to which the name supposedly refers and the nature of the name itself. Moreover, in no sutra or classical commentary at all do we see bodhisattvas who have reached the state conducive to their certain separation from suffering referred to as bodhisattvas residing in the dzambu-tree grove. Therefore the being in question is a bodhisattva who has managed to develop the first concentration level sitting at the base of a dzambu tree, and who has gained his every goal. From the point of view of his having overcome any desire for the objects of the desire realm, the bodhisattva is in no way distinguished from the non-Buddhists mentioned. His vast superiority is nonetheless reflected in the fact that giving to this single person constitutes so much greater merit than giving to the hundred others.

rows.english: If one focusses primarily on the taking of vows, and then fails in the practical aspects of keeping them seriously and restoring them when they are damaged, then there is absolutely no way that one's practice of the ethical way of life can be pure. As such it is essential that you now go on to help your new monks keep their vows well by learning to identify what constitutes breaking them. So too you must institute a regular practice of purification and restoration, whereby the monks learn to confess past errors and restrain themselves from future error, in the event that--because of one of the four factors, such as not understanding the vows properly--they should ever transgress them. They must learn never to take it lightly when they break a vow; they must be taught the proper methods of restoring vows in every instance where they are broken. In this way, and through developing a sense of shame and propriety, as well as watchfulness, awareness, and similar tools, they will come to lead a perfectly ethical way of life.

rows.english: Someone might then make the following objection. Suppose those two paths for people of lesser and medium capacity really are grave points of error for people of greater capacity. In that case, they would have to be an obstacle toward, or even in contradiction with, the path of the greater way. And then they could never constitute a method for reaching enlightenment. But the objection is unfounded. Those two paths do constitute a grave error in the path for people of greater capacity; they prevent these people from reaching enlightenment quickly. From this point of view then, these two paths are not a method for reaching enlightenment, but it's no contradiction at all to say that they constitute a method for reaching enlightenment, in the sense that they act to gradually ripen the mental continua of listeners and "self-made" Buddhas. The point about being a grave error refers primarily to details such as the state of mind where one aspires to reach a state of blissful peace for oneself alone.

rows.english: The point here is the same as in places where, for example, it's stated that the physical body is not the self. As such, the things focused upon for the two objects that are pictured in the mind during the innate form of the view of destruction are the simple "me" which serves as the basis for the workings of karma and its consequences, as well as the simple thing which is delineated as "mine." The view of destruction focuses upon these things and believes them to be a "me" and "mine" which exist by definition. Given all this, then if the "me" were to exist by definition, it would also be true that the collection of the heaps, and their continued existence, and all its components and parts, and anything completely separate from these things at all, any of them, would have to constitute what "me" refers to. The fact though is that none of these things constitutes anything of the kind. This is what is being expressed at this point.

Proving that these constitute a totally pure path that we should practice is accomplished by using the eight different forms of logic. As such there is but one main way of keeping the teachings of the victorious Buddha safe in the world, and this is to become a master of the logical forms used to prove some things and to disprove others. They are, in short, things that waste one's opportunity; you should understand that these two will cause you to fall from this spiritual way of discipline. rows.english: If we explain discounting things as being the view that something which in actuality does exist ultimately doesn't exist at all, then it would seem that we'd have to explain concocting things as being the converse; that is, as the view that something which in actuality does not exist ultimately, does exist. The position stated at this point though is that concocting things consists of holding that constructs exist by definition--which means holding them to exist ultimately. So although it's not stated clearly in the actual wording, the point of the text here is that--if something exists by definition--then it exists ultimately. Holding that constructs exist ultimately then, according to this view, constitutes the act of concocting things.

rows.english: All impure feelings of pleasure constitute the second type of suffering: the "suffering of change." We can explain this suffering as follows. rows.english: Any particular thing acting as a cause that could bring about any other thing--that is, its result--without a change could never be its transforming cause; which is to say, its material cause. It would be, for example, like a buffalo and a cow or any other such thing. And the mind and the body are just the same: they could never be for each other a material cause and the thing that the material cause produced. This is because they each come from their own material cause, and from each other only as a factor that is one together with them. They stay, for example, together--exactly like fire and melted copper. The unusual Tibetan words here about the cows refer to a buffalo and to a milk cow. [The idea being expressed is that, although a buffalo and a cow can interact and affect each other, and thus in a sense act as factors for certain details of each other's being as they coexist, they are not the kind of cause and effect for each other where one transforms into the other; that is, they are not the kind of cause and effect that seeds and their sprouts are, for example. Fire affects copper by melting it in an apparently simultaneous way, but does not itself turn into the melted copper.] 19 Selections on How Ignorant Desire Triggers Another Life The first selection is from the Overview of Dependent Origination, by Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493-1568), an eminent author of textbooks from Sera Mey Tibetan Monastery. rows.english: One may then pose another question: "Suppose the embryo in one woman's body is removed and placed in the womb of another, and the child takes birth from this woman's womb. Killing which of these two women would constitute the `immediate' misdeed?" The mother of the person in question is the former of the two women: the one whose menses he came from. Therefore killing this first woman would be the immediate misdeed; she played the principal role in providing the person a body fit for gaining freedom. We could not consider the second woman, the woman who kept the child in her womb, the child's mother--this act alone would not make hers the principal role.

rows.english: The point here is the same as in places where, for example, it's stated that the physical body is not the self. As such, the things focused upon for the two objects that are pictured in the mind during the innate form of the view of destruction are the simple "me" which serves as the basis for the workings of karma and its consequences, as well as the simple thing which is delineated as "mine." The view of destruction focuses upon these things and believes them to be a "me" and "mine" which exist by definition. Given all this, then if the "me" were to exist by definition, it would also be true that the collection of the heaps, and their continued existence, and all its components and parts, and anything completely separate from these things at all, any of them, would have to constitute what "me" refers to. The fact though is that none of these things constitutes anything of the kind. This is what is being expressed at this point.

rows.english: The wording of this particular vow says that we have committed it when we have lost our love "for living beings," using the plural.  You should understand though that we break it whenever we have lost our love for any one living being. Now exactly what is it that we have to do to commit this particular downfall?  Krishnapada explains it as follows: Those who follow the greater way must feel towards every living being the same way they would towards their only child.  They must never, for even a single instant, give up on any one of these beings.  A follower of the greater way who has divorced themselves from this powerful karmic object of a single living being no longer even deserves the name of a "follower of the greater way."  It would be like calling  a firefly "the sun." Shantipa puts it this way: The state of "love" is where we have a true desire to assure that each and every living being reaches a state of unsurpassed help and happiness: where we never, ever, give up on one of them. These two explanations of the vow amount to the same thing, and so we can say that acting in a way opposite to what is described in them as "love" would constitute the act of giving up our love. ***

To back this up he quotes [the Total Purification of Appearances]: Disparaging the teachings of non-Buddhists Takes us farther from the Angel, Appearances. While it is a negative deed if we criticize non-Buddhist schools out of a motivation to say something badly of them, it doesn't quite fit to say that these schools constitute the object towards which we commit the root downfall we're discussing here. rows.english: Here next is how the various paths of the activity class and the class of deep practice within the secret teachings are organized into the five paths and ten levels.  Consider first all the paths that occur within the period that begins with one swearing that he or she will reach enlightenment by using the path of one of these two classes, on up to the point where, due to their practice of a meditation where there are no longer any signs, they are just about to attain extraordinary insight which perceives emptiness.  All these paths together constitute the path of accumulation for the corresponding one of the two classes here.
rows.acip: SPYOD RGYUD DANG RNAL 'BYOR RGYUD KYI LAM RNAMS LAM LNGA DANG SA BCUR 'JOG TSUL NI, DE GNYIS RANG RANG GI LAM GYIS SANGS RGYAS THOB PAR DAM BCA' BA'I BLO LA BCOS MIN GYI MYONG BA THON PA NAS BZUNG STE, RANG RANG GI MTSAN MED KYI RNAL 'BYOR BSGOMS STOBS KYIS STONG NYID RTOGS PA'I LHAG MTHONG MA THOB TSUN CHAD KYI LAM RNAMS DE GNYIS RANG RANG GI TSOGS LAM DANG ,

rows.english: Consider next all the paths that occur within the period that begins with attaining extraordinary insight which perceives emptiness, and which represents a deep practice where there are no longer any signs, for the particular one of the two classes here; on up to the point where we are just about to see emptiness directly.  These paths together constitute the path of preparation for whichever one of the two classes here we are talking about. These and all the rest of the presentation for these two classes continues then to follow the same pattern as we had for the previous class.
rows.acip: DE GNYIS RANG RANG GI MTSAN MED KYI RNAL 'BYOR DU GYUR PA'I STONG NYID RTOGS PA'I LHAG MTHONG NAS STONG NYID MNGON SUM DU MA RTOGS TSUN CHAD KYI LAM RNAMS DE GNYIS RANG RANG GI SBYOR LAM YIN PA SOGS THAMS CAD SNGA MA'I RIGS 'GRE SBYAR NAS SHES PAR BYA'O,,

Are you claiming then that these qualities constitute paths that belong to the lower classes of the secret teachings?  Because isn't the way you've defined the five paths and ten levels for these classes something which is accurate?

rows.english: As for the explanation that this constitutes the ultimate form of the recitation of the diamonds, the dialectic analysis of the Combination of the Four Commentaries says, Given that this form of the recitation of the diamonds gives birth to the combination of the two, it is said to be "ultimate," with reference to the function of the reciting the diamonds.  You can also say that it is spoken of this way from the point of view of a part of what it entails; that is, even when we reach the combination of the two, we continue to practice a recitation of the diamonds which is similar to that which we do during the stage of transcendent speech.
rows.acip: DER RDOR BZLAS MTHAR THUG TU BSHAD PA NA 'GREL PA BZHI SBRAG GI MTHA' GCOD LAS, RDOR BZLAS 'DIS ZUNG 'JUG SKYED PA RDOR BZLAS KYI LAS SU BYA BA'I SGO NAS MTHAR THUG TU GSUNGS PA'AM, YANG NA ZUNG 'JUG GI SKABS SU YANG NGAG DBEN GYI SKABS DANG 'DRA BA'I RDOR BZLAS BYED PA PHYOGS GCIG LA DGONGS NAS DE LTAR BSHAD DO, ,ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR YIN NO,,

rows.english: As well as, Every instance where any of the four forms of emptiness appear to the mind from the point that one first begins to practice transcendent speech up to the point where every last one of the remaining knots at the heart are freed constitutes transcendent speech.  And in order for every last one of the remaining knots at the heart to be freed, we must use both of the outer and inner methods described above.

rows.english: Someone might come and make the following claim: Isn't it the case that there are no four forms each of bliss for the stages of where the element descends from the top, and then fills from below, where these are any one of the four forms of emptiness during the stage of transcendent mind?  Because doesn't the Sun that Illuminates the Profound say-- Here during the stage of transcendent mind, all that we speak of is the four types of bliss as the process moves in its forward progression, and the inner winds and element of enlightenment move from the upper and lower parts of the body and gather at the heart.  We do not though here speak of any four states of bliss which occur during the reversal of this progression, and which constitute the clear light.  This is because--if we were to speak of such states--then we'd have to do so relative to how the element of enlightenment splits off in stages from the heart; and in such case the winds would be shifting.
rows.acip: KHA CIG ,SEMS DBEN GYI STONG PA BZHI PO GANG RUNG DU GYUR PA'I YAS BABS DANG MAS BRTAN GYI DGA' BA BZHI BZHI MED PAR THAL, ZAB DON GSAL BA'I NYI MA LAS, SEMS DBEN SKABS 'DIR RLUNG DANG BYANG SEMS LUS KYI STOD SMAD NAS BSDUS PA'I LUGS 'BYUNG GI DGA' BA BZHI LAS 'OD GSAL GYI NGO BOR GYUR PA'I LUGS LDOG GI DGA' BZHI MI 'JOG STE, GAL TE 'JOG NA BYANG SEMS SNYING GA NAS GYES PA'I RIM PAS 'JOG DGOS PA GANG ZHIG ,DE LTAR NA RLUNG G-YO BAR 'GYUR BA'I PHYIR RO, ,ZHES GSUNGS PA'I PHYIR ZER NA

rows.english: Here the text on the stage of completion entitled The Golden Harvest of Attainments says, It would be incorrect to say that the three stages of light, proliferation, and attainment as the process reverses itself constitute the wisdom of the clear light.  Nonetheless, there is an explanation that the other three forms of bliss during this reversal of the process are the simultaneous form.  We do see, in the same way, the three of light, proliferation, and attainment spoken of as the process moves in its forward progression--and we see these three spoken of as being three of the forms of bliss, even though they are not said to be simultaneous bliss.  It does appear though that there is another point where the three forms of bliss during the forward progression are said to be simultaneous bliss. We don't find any more specific reference on this point than what is here.

rows.english: This is because, first of all, both of these paths as they are spoken of in other contexts are gross states of mind--there is no distinction drawn between them, saying that one is more subtle than the other.  Secondly, it's permissible to say that they are both states of mind in which the tendency of duality towards emptiness has been suppressed--since the two represent a single flow.  There is on the other hand a distinction between the clear light and the stage of attainment as to subtlety, and as well the difference that they constitute separate flows.  As such the two paths as spoken of in other contexts are not equivalent to the ones we have here.
rows.acip: PHYOGS GZHAN NAS BSHAD PA'I LAM DE GNYIS KA PHRA RAGS KYI KHYAD PAR MED PAR BLO RAGS PA YIN PA DANG , RGYUN GCIG YIN PAS GNYIS KA STONG PA NYID LA GNYIS SNANG NUB PA'I BLO YIN PAR BZHAG CHOG LA, 'OD GSAL DANG NYER THOB GNYIS LA PHRA RAGS KYI KHYAD PAR YANG YOD LA, RGYUN SO SO BA'I KHYAD PAR YANG YOD PAS, PHYOGS GZHAN NAS BSHAD PA'I LAM DE GNYIS DANG MI MTSUNGS PA'I PHYIR,

rows.english: Now make the offerings, but first you must bless these offerings.  To do that, you must first bless the inner offering that you will use to clear the offerings.  Now except for some differences in the Angel Man and Wife, and in the length of the ritual, the Word of the Man and the Word of the Wife constitute one body of practice; therefore the method of blessing the inner offering here is similar to that you use when you perform the ritual for Highest Bliss.

It is said that the presence of the blessings of all Buddhas in the hung letter at the heart constitutes the force of the basis, and there are other positions as well.  Our own position is that performing the practice here of going for refuge and developing the Wish represents the force of the basis.

rows.english: As for the meanings of the secret words used for the offering, argham and the rest represent the actual names of the various things that you offer.  Praticha means "to partake of, individually."  So ha here means "establish," and om ah huung constitutes the sacred letters for the three diamonds. The whole string then means "Please partake individually of the various offerings, water for drink and the rest, which are in their nature the three diamonds.  Establish Your hearts in the wisdom of inseparable bliss and emptiness."

rows.english: You can visualize all the offering Angels either with four arms or with two; aside from the extra detail, there is no difference between the two.  If you do add the detail, then picture that the first two hands hold a diamond and bell.  The remaining two hands hold a jewelled vessel which contains the appropriate offering: water for drink, and so on. The order begins with the two liquids, and then the objects of enjoyment, along with music.  After these come a mirror that can show everything in the three realms, clearly; it is red and has two faces.  Then come the rest of that set.  All these constitute the outer five objects of the senses.
rows.acip: MCHOD LHA TSANG MA PHYAG BZHI'AM GNYIS GANG BYAS KYANG RGYAS BSDUS TZAM LAS KHYAD MED PAS, RGYAS PAR NA DANG PO GNYIS RDOR DRIL, LHAG MA GNYIS KYIS RIN PO CHE'I SNOD DU RE RE NAS MCHOD YON SOGS RIM BZHIN CHU GNYIS NYER SPYOD ROL MO BCAS DANG, STONG GSUM THAMS CAD GSAL BAR 'CHAR NUS PA'I ME LONG DMAR PO NGOS GNYIS PA SOGS PHYI'I 'DOD YON LNGA DANG,

rows.english: A beautiful bodily form and so on represent inner form.  Speech, in the sense of taking up a song, is inner sound.  Sweet smells wafting from the body and mouth are inner fragrance.  A delectable taste of the tongue and lips is inner taste.  The soft feeling of the lotus and so on are inner touch.  These constitute the inner five objects of the senses. Each of these are presented to the appropriate organ of sense; of the various substances that are offered, water for drink is presented to the mouth, and so on.  The five objects of the senses are as well presented to the eye, the ear, and the like.  The effect of this is, first of all, that the Beings who are the object for our collection of virtue begin to feel a sensation of bliss related to Their sense consciousnesses.
rows.acip: GZUGS MDZES PA SOGS NANG GI GZUGS, NGAG NAS GLU LEN PA NANG GI SGRA, LUS DANG KHA NAS DRI ZHIM PO 'THUL BA NANG GI DRI, LCE DANG MA MCHU'I RO BDA' BA NANG GI RO, PADMA'I REG BYA 'JAM PA SOGS NANG GI REG BYA STE NANG GI 'DOD YON LNGA BCAS SO SO'I MCHOD RDZAS MCHOD YON ZHAL SOGS DANG, 'DOD YON LNGA SPYAN DANG SNYAN SOGS SO SOR PHUL BAS TSOGS ZHING RNAMS LA DANG POR DBANG SHES KYI 'KHOR DU GYUR PA'I TSOR BA BDE BA SKYES,

rows.english: After working with this inner wind for about seven to eleven rounds, dissolve the wind into the blue sphere as before, and then press the upper wind13 down to about five fingerwidths below the navel, and hold it there.  For now, do not draw up the lower wind.14  Keep your left hand in the gesture of meditation, and with your right hand make one circle on the knees and one fingersnap.15  Then right after that, slowly release the breath.  Practice this sequence many times--this constitutes the first short session.

rows.english: For the second short session, picture the breath rising up as a thin green stream of inner wind from the eastern sphere, and coming out through the same nostril from which you just inhaled.  It then flows back in and dissolves into that same sphere.  Hold the breath, and with your right hand make two circles on the knees and two fingersnaps.  Then let the breath out.  Doing this repeatedly constitutes this second session.
rows.acip: YANG SHAR GYI THIG LE LAS RLUNG LJANG GU NAR GYIS BYUNG BA RLUNG GANG NAS RGYU BA'I SNA SGO NAS SONG, NANG DU 'JUG PA'I TSE NAR GYIS BYUNG BA SHAR GYI THIG LER THIM PAR BSAM LA RLUNG BZUNG STE LAG PA G-YAS PAS PUS MO LA SKOR BA GNYIS DANG SE GOL GNYIS BRDAB LA RLUNG BTANG BA MANG DU BYED PA THUN CHUNG GNYIS PA DANG,

rows.english: As for the third division--the original nature of what is common to both body and mind--there are the two of the extremely subtle wind (the life-holding wind) and the mind of the clear light.  From the point of view of their being aware, these are called "mind"; from the point of view of their moving, they are spoken of as "wind."  But these are just labels put on two different aspects of the same thing; in reality the two are indivisible, like water and the ripples upon the water.  They are the extremely subtle, primal inner wind and mind that constitute the indestructible drop, and this is something which is the root, or the cause, of everything in the circle of suffering life, and everything beyond it.

rows.english: Similarly, one might practice going through the various stages of death in the same way, even long before they actually occurred. rows.english: If a person like this, as they fall off to sleep, focuses on the meditation object that we described before--or even if they do not focus on it, but rather simply maintain the deep meditative concentration they were in during their waking hours, then they will in the end be able to have their sleep itself turn into this kind of concentration. As such, this cannot constitute the authentic experience of the clear light of sleep described in the teachings of unsurpassed practice.

rows.english: When you are just about ready to wake up, then see your old body as the Holy Angel in her emanation body, a pledge being with a red color, and enter through the center tip of Her head. rows.english: You can stop it here with a phet letter, if your capacity for visualization is quite firm.  And with this you can also bring on the four forms of bliss.  This though is not something that comes on because you have gathered the two side winds into the channel of dance, and brought them to dissolve there.  As such, we can't say that this experience constitutes the ecstasy of the stage of completion.  Nor would we say that--even if you took this experience of bliss with an imaginary partner and applied it to seeing emptiness, to see your heaps and the rest as Angels--it would constitute the stage of transcendent body in the practice of the stage of completion. * * * In the same text, Je Tsongkapa describes practice with an actual partner even as we perform inner recitation (ff. 140a-140b):

rows.english: The partner that we need to make pure consists of the three of our "normal" body, speech, and mind, along with actions as a fourth.  These constitute, respectively, the things which the Great Seal, the partner of pledge, the partner of the Dharma, and the partner of deeds act to make pure.

rows.english: Suppose that you learn to perform the ritual for turning your left hand into something sacred.  Then when you use this hand to make offerings to the angels of the secret world, or anything of the like, it will be quite easy for you to bring together a very special collection of good imprints, a complete collection of those imprints which together constitute a special method of bringing on bliss and emptiness.  And because your hand has thus become extremely powerful, any other action you ever undertake with it becomes something extraordinary.

rows.english: Je Tsongkapa Lobsang Drakpa has said that we see references which state that the following five elements must be present for a practice to constitute a training of the inner winds.  (1) We must first identify a person to practice with who possesses the necessary qualifications.  (2) Then we should make them a proper vessel, through the process of empowerment.  (3) They must be keeping their pledges and vows purely, and (4) must be versed in the secret words, and secret texts.  (5) Finally, they must have a really perfect grasp of the view of emptiness.

rows.english: Here as our fifth point is a description of the vow taken for the Angel of Attainment.  Offering flowers and the like constitutes an outer offering.  The inner offering is where we perform the ceremony of blessing the inner offering, and then present it.  It is the secret offering to satiate the Angels of the secret world with the bliss that comes through union with a sacred partner.  And the offering of suchness is to use this bliss to perceive emptiness.  We must train ourselves in these offerings, as mentioned before. * * * Of all the secret commitments, the Eight Mother Vows--an important element in many different traditions of the Diamond Way, such as that of the Angel of Diamond (Vajra Yogini)-- are of course the ones which relate most to practice with a spiritual partner.  And one of the best commentaries on these vows is that of Master Damtsik Dorje: The Shining Glory of Great Bliss, a Presentation of the Eight Pledges Spoken in the Root Tantra of Highest Bliss (ACIP uncataloged data).  Here are selections on the vows, from this work.
rows.acip: LNGA PA DON GRUB KYI SDOM GZUNG NI, ME TOG SOGS PHYI'I MCHOD PA, NANG MCHOD BYIN GYIS RLABS NAS 'BUL BA NANG GI MCHOD PA, PHYAG RGYA DANG SBYAR BA'I BDE BAS DKYIL 'KHOR BA'I LHA RNAMS TSIM PAR BYED PA GSANG BA'I MCHOD PA, BDE BA DES STONG NYID RTOGS PA DE KHO NA NYID KYI MCHOD PA STE SNGAR BZHIN SLOB PA'O,

rows.english: Next make the wind melt into the sphere at the middle, and focus your mind here as well.   Close the wind within a capsule.   With your left hand, press in at this same place, at the navel.   With your right hand, rub each knee with a circling gesture once, and then snap your fingers once.   After that, release the air.   Repeat this process a hundred times or something of the like, as much as you may desire.   This brings you to the end of your first short session.   Partake of some refreshment such as chang, resting yourself but not getting up off of your meditation cushion.   All this constitutes the first session.

rows.english: All this constitutes the crucial point of freedom; the crucial point of reaching nirvana in this very life. rows.english: These "and the worldly" are said then to "provide His platform." But this alone is not what is meant by the expression “growing from something other than itself.” It is said that every existing thing has two types of essential natures; which is to say, even though they do possess a kind of essential nature, we do not accept that this constitutes an essential nature where they would grow through some nature of their own.

rows.english: A bit of the things that occur in dependence—that is, things like reflections in mirrors, or echoes—are lies; but they do make their appearance to those possessed of misunderstanding. So too a little bit of physical forms like the color blue; and things like the mind and our feelings, appear really. But the nature of things, in the sense of the way things actually are, cannot in any manner make its appearance to those who still have misunderstanding. As such, a nature to things—and forms of the deception which are themselves a lie—do not constitute deceptive reality.

rows.english: Given all this, let's look at the claim that “Objects like a reflection in a mirror, which are understood to be mistaken even by some random state of mind in the everyday world, do not constitute deceptive reality; rather, they are just basic deception.” It would appear that such statements are the chatter of people who have failed to form an understanding of how the types of reality are fixed at two, no more and no less; and of the concepts of truth & falsity relative to the beliefs of the everyday world; and of these same two concepts as they are set forth by those who follow the middle way.

rows.english: Now what is the reason that—in order to establish that a certain object is, to this particular state of mind, deceptive reality—we would have to establish that the object was lying to us? Consider how we establish the word “reality,” in the expression “deceptive reality,” in the case of something like a water pitcher. Does it refer to the state of mind, or to the object of this mind? We are not in fact establishing the object as reality; rather, we need to establish reality here in the sense of establishing that the tendency to believe that things are real itself constitutes the essence of the deception. Once we see the need to do so, we can perceive that—without applying this distinction—the object does not exist in reality, and is lying to us. The need is the key here. rows.english: What this refers to is where we accept that idea that things could exist through any nature of their own; and where something that was there before is not there afterwards—which is to say, it has stopped. This constitutes agreeing to the thing being changing; but it amounts to things simply discontinuing. Once you accept the idea that a thing could exist through any nature of its own, it doesn't matter whether you assert that it's unchanging or changing; you are still holding a viewpoint where you have fallen into the extremes of things lasting forever, or simply discontinuing altogether. This is what's being said in these lines.

rows.english: According to the first of these two positions, when a functional thing like a sprout comes to an end, all the functional entities which constitute component parts of the sprout are cancelled. At the same time, no entity other than the sprout—nothing like a water pitcher or the like—is thus actualized; and, as such, they have to say that there cannot be the slightest functional thing left here. What they are thinking is that there is nothing at all that would be fitting to point to as a classical example of this kind of stopping—neither the functional things represented by the individual doors of sense such as blue or the like; nor functioning things which are conglomerates of their components, as in the case of pitchers or the like. As such, they would say, the stopping could never itself be a functional thing.

rows.english: Here in the world then we have five different types of awareness that arise from the five different sense powers. rows.english: As such, even though the skeletons don't really exist, we do have to accept that the vivid aspect of them does exist; and that it involves form, in the same way that a reflection in the mirror does. And this means that it constitutes form within the sense door of all things, and can be referred to as an imaginary form.

rows.english: When we do seek out the creation of our projections, though, it cannot bear up under the examination of our logical mind. When we say “see” here what we mean is that we should see this thing purely: meaning unmistakenly, just as it really is. The lines here constitute a brief summary of how it is that we should come to see profound emptiness.

rows.english: There can exist, in the mind of a person on the lower way, the wisdom which realizes emptiness. It does not though constitute the perfection of wisdom. If though this wisdom does come to be imbued by this pair—by this Wish and by this intention—then their realization of emptiness thereby becomes the perfection of wisdom. This is the position we should take.

rows.english: And suppose you claim that— Even though the I doesn't exist To the perceptions of That meditation— It does indeed exist during This meditation's time. Given that this existence Exists at that point, Then what we have Is a balanced meditation On the "me"; How then Could it constitute A meditation Where no "me" Was ever there? Our minds naturally go to this idea, that even though I am not perceiving a changing "me" as I focus on its unchangeable emptiness, that "me" must be hanging out there somewhere in the area, at the time. But at the same time, the very definition of something existing is for it to be perceived by an accurate perception.

rows.wylie: gang la na, phyogs re tsam ma yin par rab 'byams gsung rab kun la lta ba'i mig tu gyur cing, skal ba bzang por gyur pa'i gdul bya thar par bgrod pa'i 'jug ngogs te lam mchog tu gyur pa'i skyes bu gsum gyi lam gyi rim pa 'di nyid, brtse ba'i thugs kyis bskyod pa ste drangs pa'i thabs mkhas kyi mdzad pa yis gdul bya la gsal bar mdzad pa'i bshes gnyen rnams la'o
rows.english: And who is it that we bow down to in this verse? It is to all of those spiritual friends who utilize a variety of skillful means to clarify these teachings to their disciples, "moved by"-compelled by-their heart's love. And what are those teachings? They are these very steps on the path, which themselves constitute the very highest of all paths for individuals of three different capacities. These steps serve as eyes to view the content of all-and not just individual pieces-of the myriad forms of high teachings. And they serve as well as an entry point for disciples of sufficient goodness to make the journey to freedom.

rows.english: That state of mind where we aspire to higher rebirths by means of giving up bad deeds, and accomplishing good deeds, constitutes the path which is shared with people of lesser capacity. And that state of mind where we aspire to freedom because we want to be liberated from the cycle of pain constitutes the path which is shared with people of medium capacity. Both of these states of mind are present in the mind stream of a bodhisattva; and both of them must be practiced by a bodhisattva.

rows.english: With that we have reached our second more general section from above, which is describing how the state of wisdom we use to realize this point constitutes the path to free ourselves from this world of pain.
